doc.title: Tom Varner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 13, 2025

title: Moving to Seattle, Heaven and Hell, and the sabbatical miniatures
summary: He married, had kids, moved to Seattle after 24-25 years in Manhattan, and composed Heaven and Hell for a tentet; then taught at Cornish for 15 years.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I want to hone in a little bit – when you were talking about your sabbatical and being on the East Coast, the shorter compositions, was this made into “Heaven and Hell”?

That was a little earlier. “Heaven and Hell” was from when I moved to – well I moved – so I’ll make it really quick. All those various things I was doing, that was in New York, go to Europe, back and forth, go blah-blah-blah. Then I got married, then I had kids, then I had two kids. And trying to get the two kids on the subway etcetera, etcetera. My wife was a Seattle native. I’d been in Manhattan for 24, 25 years and so we were like okay, and I had friends that had moved to Seattle, let’s make that move. It’ll be just better in many ways, especially for our kids and our lives, etcetera, etcetera. And it was. It’s been great. But then I had this idea for making a larger project, not a quintet, not a septet, but more like a tentet – nonet, tentet, where I could work with those ideas a little bit more. So that was a group of Seattle musicians plus the great trumpet player Russ Johnson who is now in the Milwaukee area. So some of those pieces were miniatures, that’s true. But

some of them were much more longer, thought out, composed. I was very fortunate in that a couple years earlier I was able to go to have a residency at the McDowell Colony. Oh that was heaven. Just wonderful. And a lot of the music for “Heaven and Hell” I wrote for that type of configuration. I had to adjust the instrumentation a bit. So but that was a mix of notated compositions with improv and then short takes that were really just like little 60-second meditations kind of. So later, now fast forward to another ten years, or even more – no not – yeah, something like that, I've been teaching at Cornish College of the Arts where many great people have been there and taught – Julian Priester had been there, Gary Peacock had taught there. Anyway I’ve been there for 15 years. I was very fortunate in that I was awarded a sabbatical. But I thought okay, I’m going to go back to Brooklyn and New York and Boston and Upstate New York and meet with lots of people who are near and dear to me, and just set up little – now you can get higher quality, quick set-up recording devices. So I did. I recorded 110 takes. I went a little crazy. And lots of those were very short, one to two to three minute improvisations. But I knew that all of these people were totally capable. Knew exactly what to do. I barely had to say a word. I would do something like with the great trumpet player Steven Bernstein and the trombone player Joe Fiedler. We did a brass trio. I’d say, “Okay Joe and Steven, Joe and I are pretending that we’re a bluegrass banjo. Steven, you’re the singer but with your slide trumpet. Okay? This is going to be the tempo.” That’s it. And they’d go, “Got it.” So we did. And that’s like maybe one of the first takes of that day. So a lot of things of those literally 110 tracks of lots of different – there was – I did eleven sessions. A lot of them were these little two-minute miniatures basically. With no written music. Nothing more than my verbal, “Let’s try this, let’s try that.” Sorry.
